chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Muhammad ibn Abi al-Subbah, who said:

I said to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): 'My mother gave me a gift of her share in a house. I told her that the judges do not validate this type of gift, but rather have her write it down as a sale. She said: 'Do with it whatever seems good to you, in all that you see is permissible for you.' So I took possession (of the property). Some of the heirs wanted to make me swear an oath that I had paid her the price, although I had not paid her anything. He said: 'Swear to them.'
ai.seo_question: What is the Shia juristic ruling on recording a gift as a sale to avoid judicial scrutiny, and what oath should be taken if heirs dispute it?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of *al-ta'wil* (legal interpretation) and the permissibility of *hiyal* (legal stratagems) to achieve valid outcomes within the bounds of Sharia. The Imam’s approval of recording a gift as a sale highlights the flexibility in transactional forms to satisfy judicial requirements, while the ruling to swear actual payment validates the substantive reality of the gift despite the formal fiction of a sale. This case underscores the importance of intent (*niyyah*) and the practical application of oaths in resolving inheritance disputes in Shia jurisprudence.
